title.en: The Origin of the Buffalo Society

region.en: Plains of the West where the buffalo ranges (symbolic pin on the western prairie)
region.zh: 西方水牛棲息的草原（象徵性定位於西部大草原）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 16, 'The Origin of the Buffalo Society' (1923)

summary.en: A lost hunter is adopted by the buffalo people in human form. Their evil chief drums them into murderous ten-day races for his amusement; the youth's foster mother arms him with medicine and a bow and counsels him to shoot the red spot on the chief's hand, for as a human he runs. He outlasts and kills the chief, is named deliverer, receives the buffalo healing formula - burn tobacco and call on the spirits of the buffalo - and carries the dances, songs and mysteries home, founding the Society of Buffaloes.
summary.zh: 迷路的獵人被化為人形的水牛族人收養。其惡首領擊鼓召集族人，驅使他們進行十日奪命的賽跑取樂；養母授他藥物與弓，教他射中首領手上的紅點——因他以人形奔跑。少年耗勝並誅殺首領，被尊為解放者，得授水牛療癒之語——焚菸草、呼喚水牛之靈——並將其歌舞與奧秘帶回人間，創立水牛會。

sensitivity.note: Seneca medicine-society charter myth (Parker 1923); public domain. The healing formula is given as narrative, not as operative ritual.

passages.text: A youth who had wandered out into the plains of the West lost the trail home. At sunset he saw people gathered about a fire in earnest council - and creeping near was amazed to find it was he himself who formed the subject of the discussion, and that an old lady walked directly to his hiding place: 'Come, I have adopted you. You must learn first.' The people never hunted but traveled together in bands over the prairies; the men had shaggy heads and dark hairy leggings, and he learned the dances, songs and ceremonies until he knew almost everything a tribesman knew.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 137-138; not verbatim.

passages.text: One night a far-away drum sounded, and the foster mother explained: beneath a great hill lives the great chief of all buffaloes, an evil chief; when he drums he wishes all to gather, for he is anxious for a race, and he whom the chief selects must run until death strikes away his life. 'How is it that a buffalo is your chief?' asked the youth. 'Because we are all buffaloes,' was the answer. They stampeded ten days and ten nights to the hill, many dying from exhaustion and wounds, and there the old woman gave him medicine: 'He will challenge you to a race. Take this medicine, race him to death, and shoot him in the red spot on his hand - for as a human he runs.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 138-140; not verbatim.

passages.text: The shaggy buffalo chief started the race: 'Catch me or at sunset I will trample you to the dust.' The boy ran on and on, disconcerting the chief with cries of 'Yow! Yow!' until the great beast fell with a groan - 'Shoot me, boy, shoot me!' - but the boy saw through the craft, commanded him to arise, and sent an arrow into the red spot on his hand. A great shout rent the air; the herds called him their deliverer and promised all the power the race of buffaloes could bestow: 'When you wish a balm for fear and a cure for disease, burn tobacco and call upon the spirits of the buffalo.' The youth carried the secrets home to his own people, and thus originated the Society of Buffaloes, which today exists as a power among the Seneca.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 140-141; not verbatim.

title.en: The Boy Who Could Not Understand

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 17, 'The Boy Who Could Not Understand' (1923)

summary.en: Raised in the woods by an old woman who never taught him oratory, a literal-minded boy takes every Seneca idiom of his grandfather at face value: he tears out his nails for 'leave your nails on the tree,' gouges out an eye for 'put your eyes on it,' aims at the old man's heart when told to 'shoot him here,' cooks the door, tomahawk and False Face for 'the door, the tomahawk, the false face,' kicks his uncle for 'jounce your uncle on your knee,' saws spoons in half for 'give each one half a spoon,' ties meat to his forehead, and sits all night with his legs under a doorway - 'shove your legs in the door.'
summary.zh: 由未教他辭令的老婦養於林中的男孩，把祖父的每句塞內卡慣用語都照字面執行：聽聞「把指甲留在樹上」便拔指甲插進樹皮；「把眼睛放在樹上」便剜眼；「朝這裡射」便瞄準老人心口；「把門、戰斧、假臉備好」便真的把門板拆下煮了；「在膝上顛一顛叔叔」便一腳踢倒叔叔；「每人半把匙」便把木匙鋸半；「把腿伸進門」便整夜把腿塞在門下。

sensitivity.note: Humor tale on Seneca idioms (Cornplanter 1906, Parker 1923); public domain. Parker suggests the tale may have been invented by a captive Algonkin learning Seneca.

passages.text: A boy reared in the woods by an old woman had never attended a council or learned the use of words. Sent to locate a bear tree and 'wade'ode' (leave your nails on it), he tore off his finger nails and stuck them in the bark, and proudly displayed his bleeding fingers. Told to 'put your eyes on the tree,' he gouged out one eye with a stick and hung it on the bear tree, keeping the other to find his way home. 'Oh, grandfather, why do you never say what you mean?'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 142-143; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the bear tree the grandfather patted his heart: 'shoot him here when he comes out' - and the boy aimed at the old man's heart. When the bear was dressed, the old man said he had placed 'the door, the tomahawk, the false face and the skirt' aside and told the boy to cook them and yell 'Hai-ie' when the tomahawk snapped. The boy tore the lodge door to pieces, roasted his grandfather's best stone tomahawk red-hot in the fire, and boiled a False Face mask, a breech skirt and the door splinters in a cauldron, whooping 'Hai-ie!' outside because 'it is too hot within.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 143-144; not verbatim.

passages.text: Made a secondary chief, he was told to invite 'all the tall trees, all the rough places, all the swamps, and all the high hills,' and 'jounce your uncle on your knee': he invited the trees, mountains and swamps and knocked his uncle down with a kick - for the 'tall trees' were the sachems, the 'mountains' the war chiefs, the 'swamps' the common warriors. 'Give each one half a spoon' produced twenty wooden spoons sawed in halves; 'tie it on your head and let it hang' put a rope of juicy meat on his forehead; and 'go shove your legs in the door' found him sitting all night with his legs under a stranger's doorway, until the old woman within gave him a blow with a corn pounder. When he married, his wife made him understand, and he learned many new things.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 145-146; not verbatim.

title.en: The Boy Who Lived with the Bears

region.en: Deep woods of the Seneca country (pin at Zoar Valley, Cattaraugus, New York)
region.zh: 塞內卡之地的深林（定位於紐約州卡塔勞格斯佐爾谷）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 18, 'The Boy Who Lived with the Bears' (1923)

summary.en: An unloved stepson is lured into a hole and sealed under a boulder by his foster father. The animals hold council and a bear grandmother adopts him, feeding him honey and berries and teaching him the classes of human hunters - brush-in-the-mouth, blind, heavy-stepper, swinging-mouth, and the dreaded 'four eyes' with a dog. When the true hunter fires the hollow stub, the bear mother and cubs die running but Hono' is spared, and the hunter, discovering the boy he meant to lose, repents: he never dares hunt again.
summary.zh: 飽受冷落的繼子被繼父誘入地洞，以巨石封死。眾獸集議，一位熊祖母收養了他，以蜜與莓果餵養，並教他辨識人類獵人的等級——含枝者、盲者、重步者、擺口者，以及帶犬的可怕「四眼者」。真獵人火燒空心樹時，熊母與幼熊奔逃而死，洪諾倖免；獵人認出自己原要拋棄的孩子，懺悔不已，此後再不敢狩獵。

sensitivity.note: Seneca animal-foster-parent tale (Parker 1923); public domain. The hunter taxonomy is bear-perspective folk knowledge.

passages.text: Hono' was an unloved stepson; his foster father begrudged the very food he ate. Feigning friendliness, the man lured him on a journey and pointed to a hole: 'Crawl in and catch the game. Oh you will be a big hunter now!' As Hono' crawled into the dark tunnel the opening grew dark and the entire cavern; running forward in terror he crashed his head into the stone the man had rolled into place. Outside the evil man laughed in savage glee: 'He will never push that boulder away.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 147-148; not verbatim.

passages.text: Awakened by voices, Hono' heard a council above ground discussing his fate, then the boulder rolled down the hill: 'Come out upon the earth if yet you are living.' About him on every hand were animals. 'The boy is rescued,' said a porcupine. 'Who will care for him?' Each extolled its merits until a bear woman said, 'I am old and rather surly, but I have a warm heart. I live happily in summer and sleep much in winter. I eat honey, nuts and berries.' 'Oh you will do,' shouted Hono'. She took him by the neck like a cub into a great hollow stub, fed him honey-comb and dried berries, gave him her paw to suck, and warned him that wherever he was scratched, hair would grow.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 148-149; not verbatim.

passages.text: In berry and nutting season the old bear taught him the classes of hunters: the 'brush-in-the-mouth' who chews a pine twig and gives them scent; the blind man who holds his bowl over his eyes; 'heavy stepper' who warns before he comes; 'swinging mouth' who hums his song only in his mind - for 'bears can hear singing if only thought and sung in the mind.' At last came real evil: 'a true hunter... of the class we call four eyes. He has a dog with him and no sign escapes their eyes - he is your own evil foster-father. When he cuts down the tree let me run first, and last of all, Hono', you follow.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 151-152; not verbatim.

passages.text: The hunter built a fire around the dry old stub until it crashed and fell. The bear grandmother rushed out and an arrow pierced her heart, but her ghost-body ran on; the two cubs met death in a similar way; then Hono' crawled out crying, 'Father, are you going to shoot me, too?' The hunter was greatly impressed: 'I am sorry I killed your friends... but now Age! I shall always have bad luck!' He invited the boy home, for he was afraid of the bear ghosts. He never dared hunt again, but Hono' did.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 153; not verbatim.

title.en: The Seventh Son: Hornets in a Bottle and the Witch Sisters
title.zh: 第七子：瓶中胡蜂與巫婦姊妹

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

texts.period: Told in Indian-English by Aurelia Jones Miller, from Chief Warrior (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 19, 'The Seventh Son' (1923)

summary.en: Seven brothers go east one by one to listen for wives and none returns; the seventh, dressed as a great sorcerer with milkweed hair and a bottled hornet nest, slides down a steep hill into a lodge of seven witch sisters who mean to butcher him. His uncorked hornets become warriors, the mother witch dies at their raised (unswung) tomahawk, the lodge and all its medicine burn, and evil birds fly from the burning head; the youngest witch becomes his wife, and the bones of his six brothers, resurrected in haste, come up mismated - the ancestors of crooked and lame people.
summary.zh: 七兄弟依序東行聽取妻訊，皆一去不返；第七子一身巫師裝束，髮插乳草白絲，頸掛一瓶胡蜂巢，滑下陡坡落入七位巫婦姊妹之屋，險遭宰殺。他拔開瓶塞，胡蜂化為戰士；老巫在（未揮下的）戰斧前倒斃，大屋連同法藥焚燒，邪鳥自燃燒的頭顱中飛散。最年幼的巫婦成為其妻；六位兄長的骸骨倉促復生，肢體錯配——成為日後跛殘者的遠祖。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale told in Indian-English (Parker 1923); public domain. The匆促復生/mismated-bones motif recurs in the Quilt-of-Eyes tale.

passages.text: There were seven brothers two years apart, all extra hunters, each wearing a skin skirt of the animal he had shot. The grandfather sent each in turn to listen for the women to marry, and each, hearing owl, wren, crow, rabbit, deer or cracking sticks, was told to follow the sound east and never stop - and never came back. Then the seventh son came of age, and he was a kind of a witch. He dressed in a spotted deerskin skirt with deer's hoofs rattling for a fringe, pulled out the white threads of milkweed pods and worked them into his long hair until it shined all white like a dandelion, rubbed spit on his body until it got all colors, and rolled a plugged hornet nest in his hands until it was small like a little bottle, which he fastened to his neck.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 154-156; not verbatim.

passages.text: The road grew wider and the hill steeper and slippery, and he slid down into the middle of the room of a big house where seven sisters - six old maids and one young - had the kettle ready: 'Yes, get the kettle ready. We've been waiting long enough for that animal.' They tied him to a post to butcher him, but the youngest said, 'Oh look, he isn't like the others. He has curious hair and his body shines!... Let's not kill him yet.' She pulled out the bottle's cork, and out came the hornets bump on the floor - and he, being a great witch, used his great magic, and the hornets were warriors falling out until the house was full; the hornet captain cut the strings on the post.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 156-157; not verbatim.

passages.text: The old witch mother told her youngest daughter: 'I am a big witch but he is a bigger one. If I get beaten you must burn down the house and all things in it, and have all the ashes of me and everything buried.' She rushed yelling 'Kill him!' - and a hornet-man warrior only raised his tomahawk, and she fell down dead; the oldest sister raised a knife and fell dead at a raised arm. The youngest wept and said, 'I'll take him for my husband,' and the chief hornet married them. That night a guard-star came down and sat on his sleeping eye so the five sisters thought him awake and could not kill him; in the morning he ordered the big lodge and all the medicine burned, and from the mother's bursting head up through the smoke flew all kinds of evil birds no one eats - owls, screech owls, hawks, crows, buzzards, black eagles and wild poison animals with feathers. 'Let them fly away,' said the wife: 'that's how it happened all kinds of mischief got scattered around.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 157-158; not verbatim.

passages.text: The youngest daughter showed her husband where his brothers' bones were hidden. He dug them up and smoked on them in a hurry to match them, and they came to life again - but some had long legs and some short, some broken arms, some too many fingers, some not enough ribs, because the bones were not matched the right way. 'So now that's why crooked and lame people come to be born. They are the grandchildren, way down, of the brothers.' His warriors married the reformed sisters, and the whole company built a big town; then he brought his grandparents, and uncorked his bottle to let out more warriors for them.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 158-159; not verbatim.

title.en: The Boy Who Overcame All Magic by Laughter

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 20, 'The Boy Who Overcame All Magic by Laughter' (1923)

summary.en: The world lies under a demon of enchantment. Gajihsondis, raised in a hole under a cruel wizard's bed, slays the four guardian beasts of the spring - gigantic frog, duck, beaver and the blue lizard Dagwe'non'ge - and laughs each one into weakness; he defeats owl, panther, elk and serpent guards by offering each pair a chieftainship so they kill each other. In the lodge his clothes fly off their sleeping master and a white deer (his name-genius) sails out through the smoke hole; the wizard kills and restores him, and the boy, reunited with his white self, learns that grandfather and clearing-wizard are one dual being. He frees his parents from under the ground; the wizard shrivels into a skin.
summary.zh: 世界被魔法之魔籠罩。加吉松迪斯自幼被囚於床下地洞，先後誅殺守泉的四頭巨獸——大蛙、鴨、河狸與藍蜥蜴達格威農格——並以笑聲使其力竭；再以「封一人為首領」之計令貓頭鷹、豹、麋與蛇自相殘殺。屋中熟睡的主人衣物飛離其身，白鹿（其名之精靈）自煙孔飛出；巫師殺之又復生之。少年與白色的自我合一，得知祖父與空地巫師本是同一位二重者。他自地下救出父母；巫師萎縮為一張人皮。

sensitivity.note: Seneca occult tale (Cornplanter informant, Parker 1923); public domain. Parker notes the power of laughter over wizardry is a unique element.

passages.text: The world was once visited by a demon of enchantment who bewitched all the animals, trees, lakes, rivers, boys and girls, and nobody knew they had been enchanted - only that all their wishes were thwarted. Gajihsondis lived in a hole in the ground under his grandfather's bed, whipped with burning switches. When at twelve he asked for his parents the old man growled: 'You have forced me to speak... In that spring is a terrible monster filled with great magic... But now you must learn to use a bow and arrow.' Given an arrow that could never hit its mark, the boy hit the hanging raccoon's foot anyway, then the chickadee (the first creature a child may kill), then raccoon, turkey and deer, until he declared, 'Now I am going. I shall slay the monster.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 159-162; not verbatim.

passages.text: Down the changed path he found a gigantic frog crying threats - 'Whoso comes near this spring shall die' - and shot it, laughing as he trussed it; a gigantic duck and a terrifying beaver fell the same way, and at the beautiful pool itself he hooked the blue Dagwe'non'ge, a lizard four times his own length, which bit off both his legs. Gajihsondis laughed with all his might until the beast grew weak, and bargained: 'Replace my legs and I will put you back.' The lizard conjured a man and a woman from the water to make his legs whole - and he caught them with his fish line, cut off their heads, and burned them, screech-owls bursting from the exploding skulls. 'I despise you for your lack of magic,' he told the lizard, throwing it back.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 162-164; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the clearing many white owls swooped to pluck out his eyes; being truthful, he called, 'I claim this land... but I am willing to make one of you chief with me' - and the owls quarreled and clawed each other to death, as did the two panthers, two elk and two great serpents at the path's four turnings. In the great lodge an old man fed him corn mush; as the man slept his clothing flew from him to pegs and shelves, and a white deer emerged from his breast and sailed away through the smoke hole. Fleeing at dawn, Gajihsondis was felled by the wizard's war club - 'I have killed another' - but the great crows picking the body deceived the old man, who slept.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 164-166; not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy crept back and addressed the war club: 'Stand up... I am a man and will not be denied.' It pointed to a bed of soft pelts where a sleeping maiden lay - 'I will go, but first you must slay my uncle. It is because he fears you will find me that we are all bewitched.' In the duel the old man was bound and carried home - to a lodge identical with the clearing lodge, for grandfather and wizard were one dual person. Shot three times in the back, the boy sweated in the creek-side lodge until a white clear self walked out of the dark and entered his body, becoming one with him; the grandfather's war club turned soft as wet rawhide, and the old man confessed all. Gajihsondis dug under the roots of the clearing lodge and found his mother, father and sister; the wizard died and turned into a shriveled human skin, which he rolled into a bundle and hid in the rafters. 'This is my wife,' he said. 'We shall all live in a new house.'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 167-169; not verbatim.
